passage: Counsellor's note. Jahnavi came to me at break, upset, saying that Rafiq had cheated in the relay by starting early. “It's not fair,” she said. I asked what she had seen, and she described it carefully. I told her I would check with the sports teacher. She wanted to tell the whole class, which I discouraged, but I said her concern for fairness was real. I suggested she say what she saw and leave the decision to the teacher. She nodded, still frowning. Later Rafiq said he'd misheard the starter. I will talk with both about tone next week. Ms. Kaur.

qa.q: Who did Jahnavi say had cheated in the relay?
qa.a: Rafiq.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she reported Rafiq?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair and was upset, which shows a genuine concern for fairness.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest, and why?
qa.a: She suggested Jahnavi say what she saw and leave the decision to the teacher, so the concern is heard without turning into tale-telling.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel when he learns he was reported?
qa.a: He may feel accused and defensive, since he says he misheard the starter, so tone and care matter.

grounding: A child criticises a teammate as unfair and reports rule breaking, and an adult guides tone.

passage: Thursday. Today in PE Vandana kept giving herself extra turns at the rope. I told her twice that it wasn't fair. She said I was bossy. I felt hot. I'm not trying to be bossy, I just hate it when the rules are bent. Payal said I should go to Sir, but I think I sounded like a tattletale when I did. Sir said thank you for telling him and would handle it. Later, Mummy said it's good to care about fairness, but to say it kindly first. Tomorrow I will say “Can we count turns?” before I run to Sir.

qa.q: How many times did the writer tell Vandana it wasn't fair?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did the writer feel hot when Vandana said bossy?
qa.a: The writer felt misunderstood, since the concern was about fairness and not about being in charge.

qa.q: What could the writer try tomorrow?
qa.a: Say something kind first, like “Can we count turns?” before going to Sir.

qa.q: How might Vandana see the writer's complaint?
qa.a: Vandana may feel accused and see it as bossy, which shows why tone matters.

grounding: A child criticises unfair turns and reports rule breaking, and learns tone matters to avoid sounding bossy.

passage: At the village school's kabaddi practice, Leela stopped the game for the fourth time. “Masterji! Chinmay's foot went over the line again! That's cheating!” Chinmay rolled his eyes. The others groaned. Masterji walked over. “Was it over?” he asked Chinmay. Chinmay looked. “A little. Sorry.” Masterji turned to Leela. “You were right about the line. You care about fairness, and that's good.” Leela beamed. “But four stops in ten minutes, and shouting ‘cheating’, make people stop listening. Next time, tell Chinmay calmly first: ‘Your foot's over.’ Come to me if it keeps happening, or if someone could get hurt.” Leela thought about it and nodded.

qa.q: How many times had Leela stopped the game?
qa.a: Leela had stopped the game four times.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she shouted “That's cheating”?
qa.a: Leela felt indignant and frustrated about the unfair foot over the line.

qa.q: What guidance did Masterji give Leela about tone?
qa.a: To tell Chinmay calmly first, and come to him if it keeps happening or someone could get hurt.

qa.q: How did the other players react to the stops?
qa.a: They groaned, tired of the game being stopped and of the shouting.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine fairness complaint sliding into constant reporting, and an adult guiding her on tone.

passage: At the football club in São Paulo, Kaito was captain again, and again he picked his three best friends first. Rafael, left until nearly last, marched to the coach. “It's not fair! Kaito always picks his friends. He's a cheat and a bully!” The coach raised a hand. “Hold on. Is he breaking a rule?” Rafael paused. “No. But it's unfair.” “That's a real point, and I'm glad you told me. ‘Cheat’ and ‘bully’ aren't true, though, and they make people stop listening.” Rafael's face went red. “So what do I say?” “Say, ‘Can we rotate captains, so everyone gets picked early sometimes?’” Rafael said it at the team meeting. From then on, captains rotated weekly.

qa.q: How often did captains rotate after the meeting?
qa.a: Captains rotated weekly.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling as he marched to the coach?
qa.a: Rafael felt angry and hurt at being picked nearly last again, and it seemed unfair.

qa.q: How did the coach help Rafael turn his complaint into something useful?
qa.a: He agreed the fairness point was real but asked Rafael to drop the untrue labels and suggest a rotation instead.

qa.q: What would change if Rafael had called Kaito a cheat at the team meeting?
qa.a: Kaito and his friends would probably get defensive, and the fair idea of rotating captains might have been ignored.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine fairness criticism turning into name-calling, and an adult guiding the tone into a fair proposal.

passage: Every evening at the hostel, Kalyani came to Nirmala Ma'am's office with a list. “Rupa jumped the bathroom queue. Asha had her light on after ten. Someone took two chapatis.” Nirmala Ma'am listened, then patted the chair. “Kalyani, you notice when things are unfair, and that matters. Some of these are small, though. What could you do about the queue yourself?” Kalyani frowned. “Tell Rupa?” “Yes, calmly. If someone's being hurt, or it's unsafe, or talking doesn't work, then you come to me. Always.” The next evening there was only one thing on the list: “The fire exit is blocked by trunks.” Nirmala Ma'am got up at once.

qa.q: What was blocking the fire exit?
qa.a: Trunks were blocking the fire exit.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling as she brought her list each evening?
qa.a: Kalyani felt strongly that the small rule-breaks were unfair and wanted them fixed.

qa.q: What guidance did Nirmala Ma'am give Kalyani?
qa.a: To handle small things calmly with the person first, and to come to her whenever someone is hurt, something is unsafe or talking doesn't work.

qa.q: How did Nirmala Ma'am respond to the blocked fire exit?
qa.a: She got up at once, showing that serious safety reports are exactly what she wants to hear.

grounding: Shows a child's genuine concern for fairness sliding into tale-telling, and an adult guiding when to speak to peers and when to report.

passage:
I'm Jaya, Manoj's twin sister, and I watched the whole Sunday match from the wall. When the teams were picked, Manoj said, "That's not fair. All the Class 7 boys are on one side." He was right, and Coach Bhatia swapped two players. Everybody agreed.

But then Manoj kept going. "Coach, Kunal's foot was over the line!" "Coach, Deepu took two extra balls!" "Coach, they're whispering!" By the tenth time, even his own team groaned.

Coach called him over. "You've got a good eye for fairness, Manoj. Tell me the big things. The small ones, sort out with the player, politely." I don't know if Manoj was embarrassed, but he didn't shout "Coach" again that day.

qa.q: Who swapped two players?
qa.a: Coach Bhatia.

qa.q: What might Manoj have been feeling when he kept calling "Coach"?
qa.a: Probably a strong, genuine sense that things should be fair, and some frustration; Jaya can't tell whether he felt embarrassed afterwards.

qa.q: What guidance did Coach Bhatia give on tone?
qa.a: Report the big things to the coach and sort out the small ones politely with the player, rather than telling on every little thing.

qa.q: How did Manoj's own team react by the tenth complaint?
qa.a: They got fed up and groaned, seeing it as tale-telling rather than fairness.

grounding: It is a sister's account of a child's genuine fairness complaint being upheld, then sliding into tale-telling until a coach guides his tone.
